subject: Computer Organization & Architecture (COA) & Microprocessors
exam_relevance: 12-14 questions expected in BPSC TRE CS exam

questions.question: Intel 8085 microprocessor belongs to which generation?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: 8085 is 2nd generation, 8-bit NMOS processor. 1st gen=4004(4-bit), 3rd gen=8086(16-bit).

questions.question: The maximum addressable memory of the third generation microprocessor (Intel 80286) is:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: 80286 (3rd gen) has a 24-bit address bus, giving 2^24 = 16 MB maximum addressable memory.

questions.question: Which microprocessor is considered the first commercially available microprocessor?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Intel 4004 (1971) was the first commercial microprocessor — 4-bit, 1st generation, designed for calculators.

questions.question: A microprocessor is best defined as:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Microprocessor = CPU (ALU + CU + registers) on a single IC chip. Microcontroller = computer on a single chip.

questions.question: A microcontroller is best defined as:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Microcontroller = CPU + RAM + ROM + I/O ports on a single chip (computer on a single chip), e.g., Intel 8051.

questions.question: If the last memory location is FFFFH (starting from 0000H), the size of the memory is:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: 0000H to FFFFH = 65536 locations = 64 K. A 16-bit address bus addresses 2^16 = 64 K locations.

questions.question: The term 'Tera' in computer memory sizing represents:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Tera = 2^40. Kilo = 2^10, Mega = 2^20, Giga = 2^30, Tera = 2^40, Peta = 2^50.

questions.question: Which of the following are 8-bit second-generation microprocessors?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Intel 8085, Zilog Z80, and Motorola 6800 are all classic 8-bit 2nd-generation microprocessors.

questions.question: Which generation microprocessor introduced a 32-bit architecture with 4 GB addressable memory (e.g., Intel 80386)?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: 80386/80486 (4th gen) introduced 32-bit data & address buses, giving 2^32 = 4 GB maximum addressable memory.

questions.question: The Intel 8085 microprocessor is fabricated using which technology?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: 8085 uses NMOS (N-channel Metal Oxide Semiconductor) technology and operates at 3–6 MHz.

questions.question: How many pins does the standard Intel 8085 microprocessor IC package have?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Intel 8085 comes in a 40-pin DIP package. Since 28, 32, and 64 are all wrong, (E) is correct.

questions.question: Fifth-generation 64-bit microprocessors (using 44+ address lines) can practically address memory in excess of:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: 64-bit 5th-gen processors support 16 TB+ physical memory (2^44 = 16 TB; theoretical 2^64 = 16 EB).

questions.question: Which register in the Intel 8085 serves as the accumulator?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Register A (8-bit) is the accumulator in 8085; it holds one ALU operand and stores arithmetic/logic results.

questions.question: The ALE (Address Latch Enable) pin in Intel 8085 is used to:

options.A: Enable the external data bus only
options.C: Demultiplex the lower 8-bit address from the multiplexed AD0–AD7 bus
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: ALE goes HIGH during T1 to indicate AD0–AD7 carries the lower 8 address bits so an external latch captures them.

questions.question: How many status flags are present in the Intel 8085 flag register?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: 8085 has 5 flags: Sign (S), Zero (Z), Auxiliary Carry (AC), Parity (P), and Carry (CY). None of A/B/C is 5.

questions.question: The Sign flag (S) in Intel 8085 is set to 1 when:

options.A: The result of an operation is zero
options.B: Bit D7 (MSB) of the result is 1
options.C: There is a carry from bit D3 to bit D4
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Sign flag S=1 when MSB (D7) of the 8-bit result is 1 (negative in 2's complement), and S=0 when D7=0.

questions.question: The Auxiliary Carry flag (AC) in Intel 8085 is primarily used internally for:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: AC is set on a carry from bit 3 to bit 4 (lower nibble to upper nibble) and is used by DAA for BCD adjustment.

questions.question: Which of the following are valid 16-bit general-purpose register pairs in Intel 8085?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: In 8085, the six 8-bit general-purpose registers form three 16-bit pairs: BC, DE, and HL (all of A, B, C).

questions.question: The Stack Pointer (SP) in Intel 8085 is a:

options.A: 8-bit register pointing to the top of the stack
options.B: 16-bit register pointing to the next instruction to fetch
options.C: 16-bit register pointing to the top of the stack in memory
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: SP in 8085 is a 16-bit register holding the memory address of the stack top; PUSH decrements SP, POP increments SP.

questions.question: The READY input pin of Intel 8085 is used to:

options.A: Insert wait states to synchronize with slow memory or I/O devices
options.B: Reset the microprocessor to initial state
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: When READY is LOW, 8085 enters WAIT states until the slow memory/I/O pulls READY HIGH.

questions.question: In Intel 8085, which pins form the multiplexed lower address and data bus?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: AD0–AD7 carries the lower 8-bit address during T1 and 8-bit data during T2–T3; A8–A15 carries upper address bits.

questions.question: Which of the following are programmer-accessible 8-bit general-purpose registers in Intel 8085?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: 8085 has 6 programmer-accessible 8-bit general-purpose registers: B, C, D, E, H, and L (all of A, B, C).

questions.question: When RESET IN (active LOW) is activated in Intel 8085, the Program Counter (PC) is initialized to:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Activating RESET IN resets PC to 0000H, so execution starts at address 0000H. None of A/B/C is 0000H.

questions.question: The HOLD and HLDA pins of Intel 8085 are used for:

options.A: Direct Memory Access (DMA) — HOLD requests buses, HLDA acknowledges
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: DMA controller asserts HOLD to request the system bus; 8085 floats buses and replies with HLDA.

questions.question: Which hardware interrupt of Intel 8085 has the highest priority?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: TRAP has the highest priority in 8085. Priority order: TRAP > RST 7.5 > RST 6.5 > RST 5.5 > INTR.

questions.question: The TRAP interrupt in Intel 8085 is:

options.A: Non-maskable and both edge and level triggered
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: TRAP is the only non-maskable 8085 interrupt and is both edge- and level-triggered (vectors to 0024H).

questions.question: Which hardware interrupt of Intel 8085 has the lowest priority?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: INTR has the lowest priority among 8085 hardware interrupts. Since INTR is not listed in A/B/C, (E) is correct.

questions.question: In Intel 8085, the RST 7.5 interrupt is:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: RST 7.5 is rising-edge-triggered and internally latched; RST 6.5 and RST 5.5 are level-triggered.

questions.question: Which of the following hardware interrupts in Intel 8085 are maskable using SIM/DI instructions?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: RST 7.5, RST 6.5, and RST 5.5 (plus INTR) are all maskable interrupts in 8085; only TRAP is non-maskable.

questions.question: When RST 7.5 interrupt is acknowledged by Intel 8085, the Program Counter jumps to which vector address?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Vector addresses: TRAP=0024H, RST 5.5=002CH, RST 6.5=0034H, RST 7.5=003CH (7.5 × 8 = 60 = 3CH).

questions.question: Which Intel 8085 instruction reads the interrupt mask bits, pending interrupts, and the SID pin into the accumulator?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: RIM (Read Interrupt Mask) reads mask status of RST 5.5/6.5/7.5, pending flags, IE flag, and Serial Input Data (SID).

questions.question: Which statement accurately describes the INTR pin in Intel 8085?

options.A: It is a non-vectored, maskable interrupt requiring an external INTA handshake
options.B: It has higher priority than TRAP
options.C: It cannot be disabled by the DI instruction
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: INTR is maskable (disabled by DI), lowest priority, and non-vectored — external hardware supplies RST/CALL on INTA.

questions.question: The Intel 8086 microprocessor has what size data bus and address bus?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Intel 8086 has a 16-bit data bus and a 20-bit address bus, allowing 2^20 = 1 MB of physical memory.

questions.question: What is the maximum physical memory directly addressable by the Intel 8086 microprocessor?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: 8086 has a 20-bit address bus, so max memory is 2^20 = 1 MB (00000H–FFFFFH). None of A/B/C equals 1 MB.

questions.question: In Intel 8086, a 20-bit physical address is calculated from segment and offset registers as:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Physical Address = Segment × 16 (shifted left by 4 bits / 1 hex digit) + Offset, producing a 20-bit address.

questions.question: In Intel 8086, which segment and offset pair is used to locate the next instruction to fetch?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: CS (Code Segment) holds the segment base and IP (Instruction Pointer) holds the offset of the next instruction.

questions.question: Which of the following are valid 16-bit segment registers in Intel 8086?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Intel 8086 has four 16-bit segment registers: CS, DS, SS, and ES (all of A, B, C are valid).

questions.question: In Intel 8086, the Bus Interface Unit (BIU) is responsible for:

options.A: Fetching instructions into the queue and managing bus transfers
options.B: Setting and clearing ALU status flags only
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: BIU calculates 20-bit physical addresses, fetches instructions into the prefetch queue, and performs bus reads/writes.

questions.question: The Execution Unit (EU) of Intel 8086:

options.A: Decodes and executes instructions taken from the BIU prefetch queue
options.C: Manages the external address and data buses directly
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: EU decodes and executes instructions fetched by BIU, allowing fetch and execute to overlap (2-stage pipelining).

questions.question: If CS = 2000H and IP = 0500H in Intel 8086, the physical address of the next instruction is:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Physical address = CS × 16 + IP = 2000H × 10H + 0500H = 20000H + 0500H = 20500H.

questions.question: The Extra Segment (ES) register in Intel 8086 is used by default for:

options.C: Destination operand in string operations (with DI)
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: ES:DI addresses the destination in string instructions (MOVS, STOS, SCAS, CMPS); SS:SP handles the stack.

questions.question: What is the capacity of the internal instruction prefetch queue in the Intel 8086 BIU?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Intel 8086 has a 6-byte instruction prefetch queue (8088 has 4 bytes). None of 2, 4, or 8 bytes is 6.

questions.question: Which register always holds the address of the next instruction to be fetched?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: PC holds the address of the next instruction to execute and is incremented automatically after fetching.

questions.question: The Instruction Register (IR) in a CPU is used to:

options.A: Hold the address of the next instruction
options.B: Hold the currently fetched instruction while it is decoded and executed
options.C: Store the result of ALU operations
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: IR holds the instruction word fetched from memory so the Control Unit can decode its opcode.

questions.question: The correct sequence of stages in the basic instruction cycle is:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Basic instruction cycle: Fetch instruction from memory → Decode opcode in CU → Execute operation.

questions.question: Which CPU register temporarily holds the data word being transferred to or from main memory?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: The Memory Buffer/Data Register (MBR/MDR) holds data transferred to/from memory. None of A/B/C is MBR/MDR.

questions.question: In Von Neumann architecture, program instructions and data are stored:

options.B: In the same shared main memory
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Von Neumann architecture uses a single shared memory and bus for instructions and data (stored-program concept).

questions.question: Harvard architecture differs from Von Neumann architecture by using:

options.A: Separate memory and buses for instructions and data
options.C: A single memory for both instructions and data
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Harvard architecture has separate instruction and data memories/buses, enabling simultaneous instruction fetch and data access.

questions.question: The Accumulator (ACC) register in a CPU is used to:

options.A: Store the base address for indexed addressing
options.B: Point to the top of the stack
options.C: Hold one operand and store the result of ALU operations
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: ACC supplies one input operand to the ALU and receives the output result in accumulator-based CPUs.

questions.question: What does the Control Unit (CU) of a CPU generate?

options.A: Control signals to direct CPU and memory operations
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: CU generates both control signals (A) and timing signals (B); ALU produces arithmetic results (C).

questions.question: The Memory Address Register (MAR) holds:

options.B: The address of the memory location currently being accessed
options.C: Data read from or to be written to memory
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: MAR holds the memory address placed on the address bus during a read or write cycle; MBR holds the data.

questions.question: In a standard downward-growing stack, a PUSH operation:

options.A: Increments SP and reads data from memory
options.B: Decrements SP and writes data to the new stack top address
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Stack grows downward from high to low addresses: PUSH decrements SP then stores data; POP reads then increments SP.

questions.question: In which addressing mode is the operand value directly specified inside the instruction itself?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: In immediate addressing, the constant operand is embedded in the instruction (e.g., MVI A, 05H); no memory lookup needed.

questions.question: Which is the most common addressing technique used in basic computer instruction sets?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Direct (Absolute) addressing specifies the operand's memory address directly in the instruction and is the most common technique.

questions.question: Which addressing mode requires two memory accesses to fetch the operand (first for a pointer address, second for the data)?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: In memory indirect addressing, the address field points to a memory word holding the effective address of the operand.

questions.question: In register addressing mode, the operand is located in:

options.C: A CPU register specified in the instruction
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Register addressing fetches the operand directly from a CPU register (e.g., MOV A, B), requiring zero memory accesses.

questions.question: In indexed addressing mode, the effective address is calculated as:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Indexed addressing computes EA = Index Register + displacement, ideal for stepping through array elements.

questions.question: Relative addressing mode calculates the effective address by adding the signed displacement to the:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Relative addressing computes EA = PC + signed offset, commonly used in branch instructions for position-independent code.

questions.question: In Intel 8085, the instruction 'MVI A, 32H' uses which addressing mode?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: MVI A, 32H loads immediate data 32H into A, so it uses Immediate addressing — none of A/B/C.

questions.question: Base register addressing mode is primarily used for:

options.A: Program relocation and accessing fields of data records
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: EA = Base Register + offset; changing the base register relocates a whole segment/record in memory.

questions.question: Which of the following 8085 instructions use Implied (Implicit) addressing mode?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: CMA, RAL, and STC all act on an implicit operand (A or CY) determined by the opcode alone; all three are implied.

questions.question: In Intel 8085, the instruction 'LDA 2050H' uses which addressing mode?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: LDA 2050H places the 16-bit memory address 2050H directly in the instruction -> Direct addressing.

questions.question: The correct order of memory hierarchy from fastest to slowest access speed is:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Speed decreases from CPU outward: Registers (fastest) → Cache → Main Memory (RAM) → Hard Disk (slowest).

questions.question: As we move down the memory hierarchy from registers to secondary storage:

options.A: Both capacity and cost per bit decrease
options.B: Capacity increases and cost per bit decreases
options.C: Capacity decreases and cost per bit increases
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Moving from registers toward disk: storage capacity increases, access time increases, and cost per bit decreases.

questions.question: Virtual memory allows programs larger than physical RAM to execute by using:

options.B: ROM chips for writable program pages
options.C: Secondary disk space (paging/swap area) as an extension of RAM
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Virtual memory maps pages between RAM and disk swap space, giving processes a large logical address space.

questions.question: Buffer registers in a computer system are used to overcome:

options.A: Differences in data transfer rates between devices
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Buffer registers temporarily hold data to smooth out speed mismatches between CPU, memory, and slower I/O devices.

questions.question: Which of the following memory types is BOTH volatile AND requires periodic refreshing?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: DRAM is volatile and needs capacitor refresh. SRAM needs no refresh; ROM and Flash are non-volatile.

questions.question: The principle of locality of reference, which makes cache memory effective, includes:

options.A: Temporal locality (recently accessed items are likely to be reused soon)
options.B: Spatial locality (items near recently accessed addresses are likely to be accessed)
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Locality of reference has two forms: temporal locality (A) and spatial locality (B). Both make caching effective.

questions.question: SRAM is preferred over DRAM for CPU cache memory primarily because SRAM:

options.A: Has higher bit density per chip
options.B: Is faster and requires no refresh circuitry
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: SRAM uses flip-flops, making it much faster than capacitor-based DRAM and eliminating refresh overhead.

questions.question: ROM (Read Only Memory) is classified as:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: ROM is directly addressable by the CPU (primary memory) and retains contents without power (non-volatile).

questions.question: The primary purpose of cache memory is to:

options.B: Provide large archival storage at low cost
options.C: Bridge the speed gap between fast CPU and slower main memory (RAM)
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Cache is a small, fast SRAM between CPU and RAM that lowers average memory access time using locality.

questions.question: In direct-mapped cache, each block of main memory maps to:

options.B: Any cache line in the entire cache
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Direct mapping assigns each block to (block_no mod cache_lines) — exactly one line; simple hardware, higher conflicts.

questions.question: Which cache mapping technique allows a main memory block to be placed in ANY cache line?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Fully associative cache allows a block in any line, eliminating conflict misses at the cost of searching all tags.

questions.question: Set-associative cache mapping is a compromise between:

options.A: Direct mapping and fully associative mapping
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Set-associative maps a block to one set (like direct) and lets it occupy any line in that set (like associative).

questions.question: In a write-through cache policy:

options.A: Writes go only to cache and main memory is updated upon eviction
options.B: Every write updates both cache and main memory simultaneously
options.C: Writes go only to main memory, bypassing cache
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Write-through updates cache and RAM together on every write, keeping memory consistent at the cost of bus traffic.

questions.question: Which control bit is needed in a write-back cache to indicate whether a cache line has been modified?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: In write-back cache, a dirty bit marks modified lines so they are written back to RAM only when evicted.

questions.question: If cache hit ratio is 0.9, cache access time is 10 ns, and main memory access time is 100 ns, the effective access time under simultaneous (parallel) access is:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Under parallel access: EMAT = h × Tc + (1 - h) × Tm = 0.9 × 10 + 0.1 × 100 = 9 + 10 = 19 ns.

questions.question: Under the LRU (Least Recently Used) cache replacement policy, which block is evicted on a miss?

options.A: The block most recently loaded into cache
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: LRU evicts the block that has not been accessed for the longest time. None of A/B/C describes LRU.

questions.question: The standard 5 stages of a classic instruction pipeline in order are:

options.A: Fetch (IF) → Execute (EX) → Decode (ID) → Write Back (WB) → Memory (MEM)
options.B: Decode (ID) → Fetch (IF) → Execute (EX) → Memory (MEM) → Write Back (WB)
options.C: Fetch (IF) → Decode (ID) → Execute (EX) → Memory (MEM) → Write Back (WB)
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Classic 5-stage RISC pipeline order: IF → ID → EX → MEM → WB.

questions.question: The ideal speedup of a k-stage pipeline over non-pipelined execution for a large number of instructions is:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Speedup S = (k × n) / (k + n - 1), which approaches k as the number of instructions n becomes large.

questions.question: A RAW (Read-After-Write) data hazard occurs in pipelining when:

options.A: Two instructions require the same hardware unit simultaneously
options.B: An instruction tries to read a register before a prior instruction writes to it
options.C: A branch instruction changes the PC
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: RAW (true dependency) occurs when a subsequent instruction needs a result not yet written back by an earlier one.

questions.question: Control (branch) hazards in a pipeline are caused by:

options.C: Branch or jump instructions changing sequential PC flow
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Control hazards arise from branches/jumps because the next PC isn't resolved until EX/ID while IF fetches sequentially.

questions.question: Operand forwarding (bypassing) in a pipeline is used to resolve:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Forwarding routes ALU/MEM results directly to a dependent instruction's EX input, avoiding RAW pipeline stalls.

questions.question: Which of the following are standard categories of pipeline hazards?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: The three classic pipeline hazard types are structural (resource), data (dependency), and control (branch) hazards.

questions.question: Branch prediction is used in modern pipelined processors primarily to minimize stalls from:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Branch prediction predicts branch outcome/target early in IF so the pipeline keeps fetching, reducing control stalls.

questions.question: How many clock cycles does an ideal 5-stage pipeline take to execute 100 instructions (1 cycle per stage, no hazards)?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Total cycles = k + n - 1 = 5 + 100 - 1 = 104 cycles. None of 500, 100, or 105 is 104.

questions.question: Booth's algorithm in computer arithmetic is used for:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Booth's algorithm multiplies signed binary numbers in 2's complement by recoding runs of 1s to reduce additions.

questions.question: In a pipelined processor, a 'pipeline bubble' (NOP stall) is inserted when:

options.A: The processor doubles its clock frequency
options.B: No instructions remain in main memory
options.C: A dependency (such as a load-use data hazard) cannot be resolved by forwarding alone
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: A bubble (stall/NOP) delays dependent instructions by one or more cycles when forwarding cannot supply the data in time.

questions.question: The method of accessing I/O devices in which the CPU repeatedly checks the device status flag is called:

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: In programmed I/O (polling), the CPU stays in a busy-wait loop checking the status register until the device is ready.

questions.question: In interrupt-driven I/O, the CPU is freed from busy-waiting because:

options.A: All I/O data bypasses memory via cache
options.B: The CPU continuously polls the status register
options.C: The I/O interface sends an interrupt signal to the CPU only when ready
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Interrupt-driven I/O lets the CPU execute other tasks until the I/O module signals readiness via an interrupt.

questions.question: Which I/O technique transfers large blocks of data directly between peripherals and RAM without continuous CPU involvement?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: DMA controller takes over the system bus to transfer blocks directly between I/O and RAM, interrupting CPU only at completion.

questions.question: Which of the following statements are true about Memory-Mapped I/O?

options.A: I/O ports share the same address space as main memory
options.B: Standard memory instructions (LOAD/STORE/MOV) are used to access I/O devices
options.C: Dedicated IN and OUT instructions are strictly mandatory
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: In memory-mapped I/O, I/O shares memory address space (A) and uses regular memory instructions (B); IN/OUT is for isolated I/O.

questions.question: In Isolated (Port-Mapped) I/O, peripheral ports are accessed using:

options.B: A separate I/O address space with dedicated IN and OUT instructions
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Isolated I/O separates memory and I/O address spaces, using special IN/OUT instructions (e.g., 8085 and x86 I/O ports).

questions.question: In DMA 'cycle stealing' mode:

options.A: The CPU is permanently halted until power-off
options.B: The DMA controller borrows one bus cycle at a time from the CPU to transfer a word
options.C: CPU cache lines are overwritten by I/O hardware
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Cycle stealing lets DMA take the bus for one memory cycle per word transfer, minimally slowing the CPU.

questions.question: RISC (Reduced Instruction Set Computer) architecture is characterized by:

options.A: Arithmetic instructions that directly modify main memory operands
options.B: Variable-length instructions and microprogrammed control unit
options.C: Fixed-length instructions, load-store model, and hardwired control unit
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: RISC uses fixed-width instructions, hardwired control, a large register file, and load-store memory access (~1 CPI).

questions.question: CISC (Complex Instruction Set Computer) architecture typically features:

options.A: Fixed-length instructions with single-cycle execution for all instructions
options.B: Load-store architecture with no memory operands in ALU instructions
options.C: Variable-length instructions, many addressing modes, and microprogrammed control
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: CISC uses variable-length multi-cycle instructions, rich addressing modes, and microprogrammed control (e.g., x86).

questions.question: Which of the following processor architectures follow the RISC design philosophy?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: ARM (Advanced RISC Machine), MIPS, and SPARC are all classic RISC architectures.

questions.question: Which of the following is a well-known example of a CISC architecture?

options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: Intel x86 (IA-32 / x86-64) is the classic CISC ISA with variable-length instructions; MIPS and ARM are RISC.

questions.question: In a load-store (RISC) architecture, which instructions are permitted to access main memory?

options.A: All arithmetic ADD and SUB instructions
options.C: None — RISC processors cannot access main memory
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: In load-store (RISC) architecture, only dedicated LOAD and STORE instructions access memory; ALU ops use registers.

questions.question: Compared to CISC, a key performance advantage of RISC is:

options.A: Simpler fixed-length decoding enabling hardwired control and ~1 CPI pipelining
options.B: Using far fewer CPU general-purpose registers
options.C: Fewer total instructions per compiled program
options.D: More than one of the above

questions.explanation: RISC's simple fixed-format instructions allow hardwired control and deep pipelining (~1 CPI), though programs have more instructions.
